title: Distil water on a stove with a copper coil
summary: A pot, a loose lid with an outlet and a clean copper coil cooled in snow or cold water turn salty, nitrate-laden or metal-laden water into drinking water. It does not remove fuel, solvents or other chemicals that boil off with the water, it burns several times the fuel of plain boiling, and a still with a sealed lid or a blocked coil can burst and scald.

materials.item: Pot with a lid, stainless steel or enamel, 5–20 L; a lid that only sits on, never one that clamps or locks
Soft copper tube, as wide as you can get (6–10 mm, 1/4–3/8 in), new or from a clean water line; never a heater core, radiator or refrigeration line
Compression or bulkhead fitting certified low-lead, to take the tube through the lid, with a washer each side
Short length of food-grade silicone hose, a loose push-on fit with no clamp, to join the lid fitting to the coil
Bucket or tub for the cooling bath, filled with snow or cold water
Clean glass jar or stainless steel container to catch the distilled water
Activated carbon post-filter for a doubtful feed
Heat: wood stove top, electric hot plate or induction ring indoors; a camp stove only outdoors

steps.text: Decide whether you need a still. It earns its fuel only on water that is salty, high in nitrate or holds metals such as lead (UNL distillation, Purdue WQ-12). Boiling won't fix those, and boiling nitrate water makes it worse (AHS nitrate). For germs alone, a 1 minute rolling boil does the job on a fraction of the fuel (Ready.gov water); boil longer at altitude, as in [Water filters](#guides/reference_water_filters).

Settle or strain the feed water, and smell it. If you know or suspect fuel, solvent or other chemicals in it (a smell, a sheen, or a source like a flooded garage, a spill, a farm or an industrial site), don't distil it: volatile chemicals such as benzene and toluene, and some solvents and pesticides, come over with the steam (UNL distillation, Purdue WQ-12).
steps.warn: Heated fuel gives off vapour that can reach the flame. Find other water; see [Handle and store fuel safely](#guides/safety_fuel_handling).

steps.text: Get the coil: new soft copper tube, or tube from a clean drinking-water line. Flush it with clean hot water until it runs clear.
steps.warn: Never a car radiator or heater core (they held glycol antifreeze, and many are joined with lead-tin solder: SAE solder paper, NIOSH radiator solder), a fridge, freezer or air-conditioner line (compressor oil: ACCA lines), or joints made with old plumbing solder (Health Canada lead).

steps.text: Drill the lid for the fitting and deburr the hole with a file. Fit the tube through it with a washer each side, and join the lid fitting to the coil with a short, loose push-on length of food-grade silicone hose, with no clamp or wire. A rigid pipe from the lid into a fixed coil would hold the lid down, so the hose must be able to flex or slip off and let the lid lift.
steps.warn: Never clamp, tape, wire or weight the lid down. If the coil blocks, the lid must be able to lift and let the steam out: see [Heating sealed containers](#browse/hazards/sealed_heating).

steps.text: Run the tube downhill all the way from the lid, coil it through the cooling bucket, and bring the end out open over the jar. No dips, kinks or valves anywhere, and the end never under water.
steps.warn: A dip fills with condensed water and can block the steam. A closed end or a valve lets pressure build, and a boiler that fails lets its energy go violently (National Board bomb).

steps.text: Pack the cooling bucket with snow or cold water. Each litre you distil gives up enough heat to melt roughly 7–8 kg of snow, so keep topping it up (HyperPhysics phase, HyperPhysics specific heat). In hard frost use a slush of snow and water rather than dry snow packed round the coil, and don't let the outlet end sit in freezing air: water can freeze in the coil and block the way out for the steam.
Fill the pot only about halfway, as FEMA's cup method does (Ready.gov water). The headroom should keep splashes and foam from reaching the coil (our reasoning).

Bring it to a steady boil, then turn the heat down to the least that keeps it going. Watch the outlet: it should drip or trickle water. Steam puffing out of the end means the coil needs more snow or the pot less heat. On a wood stove, slide the pot to a cooler spot rather than turning it down. Keep your face and hands clear of the outlet, because steam scalds. If the lid starts to jump or steam hisses from under it, the coil is blocked or too small: take the pot off the heat and let it settle before you touch anything.
Throw away the first half litre (about a pint) that comes through: it rinses the coil and carries off some volatile chemicals (UNL distillation).

Never let the pot boil dry. Stop with a good layer of water still in it, and pour the leftover out well away from your well, the water you collect and the garden: it holds everything you removed, concentrated (UNL distillation).
steps.warn: If it does boil dry, turn off the heat and let the pot cool before any water goes in.

steps.text: Turn the heat off and let the boiling stop before you touch the lid, then lift it tilted away from you.
steps.warn: Steam scalds worse than boiling water: as it turns back to water on skin it gives up about 2,256 kJ per kg (HyperPhysics phase). Cool a scald under cool running water for 10 to 20 minutes, with no ice (HealthLink BC burns).

steps.text: Keep the distilled water covered in clean containers, and use clean hands and cups. An idle outlet can let bacteria back in (UNL distillation), so boil or chlorinate the first water after the still has sat for days.
Descale the pot when a crust builds: soak with a half-and-half vinegar and water solution, then rinse (UNL distillation).

notes:
## What a still does and doesn't remove
Distilling is boiling water and catching the steam as it cools back to water. The steam leaves most dissolved things behind in the pot (UNL distillation).

| Problem | Distilled? | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Salt (sodium), hardness, fluoride, nitrate | Yes, nearly all | UNL distillation |
| Metals such as lead, iron | Yes | Purdue WQ-12, UNL distillation |
| Germs | Boiling kills bacteria and some viruses; FEMA says distilling also removes germs that resist boiling and chlorine | Purdue WQ-12, Ready.gov water |
| Fuel, solvents, benzene, toluene, some pesticides | **No.** Volatile chemicals boil off with the water and come over with the steam; the sources name benzene, toluene, some pesticides and volatile solvents | UNL distillation, Purdue WQ-12 |
| Mud and cloudiness | Stays in the pot; settle it first anyway | |

The chemical gap is the one that bites. Commercial distillers fight it with gas vents, fractional columns or a carbon filter on the output. With none of those, throwing away the first half litre or so may remove some of the volatile chemicals (UNL distillation). That's a partial fix, not a cure: water that smells of fuel or solvent needs a different source. If you suspect a weaker chemical problem, run the distillate through activated carbon afterwards (UNL distillation); see [Water filters](#guides/reference_water_filters).

## When a still is worth it
- **Yes:** brackish or salty well water, seawater, road-salt meltwater, water with lead from old plumbing, and wells high in nitrate. Canada's limit is 45 mg/L of nitrate (10 mg/L as nitrate-nitrogen); Alberta Health Services lists distillation as a fix, and warns that **boiling raises the nitrate level**, because water leaves and the nitrate stays (AHS nitrate).
- **No:** water that only needs germs killed. A rolling boil for 1 minute does that (Ready.gov water) for about a sixth of the fuel (see below). Clear it first, then boil or chlorinate: [Two-bucket gravity filter](#guides/build_gravity_water_filter).
- **No:** water with fuel, solvent or industrial chemicals in it. Distilling won't fix it.

## The coil: what to use and what never to use
Use new soft copper tube, or tube cut from a cold drinking-water line you know. Join it with compression fittings rather than solder, and choose fittings certified low-lead: brass faucets, valves and fittings can contain some lead (Health Canada lead).
- **Never a car radiator or heater core.** They held glycol antifreeze, which is poisonous (see the [chemical hazard](#browse/hazards/chemical)), and radiators and heater cores are often soldered with lead-tin solder (SAE solder paper, NIOSH radiator solder). Radiator repair has long been a known source of lead exposure from soldering (CDC radiator lead).
- **Never a fridge, freezer or air-conditioner line.** Refrigeration piping is sized to carry compressor lubricant round the system with the refrigerant (ACCA lines), so a salvaged line is likely to hold oil (our inference).
- **Never old soldered plumbing joints.** Canada allowed lead in plumbing solder until 1986, and brass fittings and valves can hold some lead (Health Canada lead). Removing lead is one of the reasons to distil; don't put it back on the way out.

## Never seal it
A still is a boiler. If the steam has nowhere to go, the pressure builds until something gives, and water that flashes to steam takes about 1,600 times the room it did as water (National Board bomb). So:
- the lid only sits on: no clamps, wire, tape or weights, and no rigid pipe from the lid into a fixed coil (join them with a loose push-on hose so the lid can lift);
- no valve, tap or cap anywhere on the steam side;
- the line runs downhill with no dips, so condensed water drains instead of plugging it;
- the outlet stays open to the air, above the water in the jar, and in hard frost doesn't freeze shut (slush in the bath, outlet end kept out of freezing air).

Don't build a still on a pressure cooker, a kettle with a locking lid or anything else made to hold pressure: a plain pot with a loose lid lets the steam out, as long as nothing holds the lid down and nothing blocks the coil. See [Heating sealed containers](#browse/hazards/sealed_heating).

## How much water, for how much fuel
The physics sets a floor. Warming 1 litre from 0 °C to the boil takes about 0.42 MJ; turning it to steam takes another 2.26 MJ (HyperPhysics specific heat, HyperPhysics phase). So **distilling a litre takes about 2.7 MJ (0.74 kWh), more than six times what it takes just to bring it to the boil.** Starting from snow adds another 0.33 MJ to melt it (HyperPhysics phase).

No stove gets all its heat into the pot. ENERGY STAR puts gas cooktops at about 32 %, electric resistance at 75–80 % and induction at about 85 % (ENERGY STAR cooktops). Worked from those figures (our arithmetic, not measured):

| Heat source | Rough yield | How it's worked out |
|---|---|---|
| 1,100 W countertop distiller | 1 US gal (3.8 L) in about 3 hours | UNL's worked example (UNL distillation) |
| 1,500 W hot plate | about 1.5 L an hour | 1.5 kW × 77 % ÷ 0.74 kWh per litre |
| Electricity, any | about 1 kWh per litre | 0.74 kWh ÷ 75–80 % |
| Propane burner | about 3 L per litre of liquid propane | 25.5 MJ per litre of propane (CER conversion) × 32 % (gas cooktop) ÷ 2.7 MJ |

Real setups with an open pot, wind and a cold kitchen do worse. Plan on a family's drinking water, not its washing water. A pot on a wood stove that's already heating the house uses heat you're making anyway, and can run all day.

## Burners and air
Camp stoves, propane burners and barbecues belong outdoors: indoors they make carbon monoxide (see the [open flame hazard](#browse/hazards/open_flame)). Indoors, use a properly vented wood stove, an electric hot plate or an induction ring. See [Cooking indoors](#guides/reference_cooking_indoors) and [Carbon monoxide](#guides/safety_carbon_monoxide).

## The cup-in-the-lid method
With no tube at all: fill a pot halfway, tie a cup to the lid's handle so it hangs upright when the lid is upside down, clear of the water, and boil for 20 minutes. What drips off the lid into the cup is distilled (Ready.gov water). It works, but it makes very little for the fuel. Wear oven gloves: the lid and cup are at steam temperature.

## Solar stills
A solar still is a shallow tray of water under sloped glass or clear plastic; the sun evaporates it and it condenses on the cover. Output is small. In New Mexico tests of small insulated, glass-covered stills with no concentrating lens, a day's output ran from about 1.4 to 2.8 L per square metre of basin, 1.6 in the base case (Reclamation solar still). That was desert sun; expect much less from short, low winter days in Canada. Treat it as a summer top-up, not a supply.

## Looking after it
- Scale builds on the pot bottom. Soak it with half vinegar, half water, then rinse (UNL distillation).
- Keep the outlet and jar clean and covered; an idle distiller can let bacteria in through the outlet (UNL distillation).
- Distilled water tastes flat because the minerals and oxygen are gone (Purdue WQ-12).
